justice: Wide, flat sidewalks provide basic physical accessibility for wheelchair users and older adults.
The absence of tactile paving (blind tracks) on the sidewalks severely reduces fairness for visually impaired individuals.
Parked vehicles occupying the edges of the non-motorized lanes reduce the equitable distribution of spatial resources for pedestrians and cyclists.
safety: The lack of separated, protected bike lanes forces cyclists and adolescents to share space with parked and moving motor vehicles, increasing collision risks.
Long, wide driving lanes without visible traffic calming measures may encourage driver speeding, reducing crossing safety for older adults and disabled persons.
Frequent and prominent streetlights provide good visibility for nighttime safety and enhance social surveillance (eyes on the street) for teenagers.
livability: Continuous ground-floor commercial storefronts provide convenient access to daily necessities, supporting the daily routines of older adults and local residents.
The integration of shopfronts and wide sidewalks creates a potentially vibrant community atmosphere for all social groups.
The complete lack of public benches or gathering spaces limits outdoor social interaction and leisure opportunities for the elderly and adolescents.
sustainability: Very sparse and young street trees provide minimal ecological benefits, shade, or green infrastructure.
There are no visible public transit shelters or dedicated cycling infrastructure to actively encourage low-carbon travel among users.
Extensive impermeable asphalt and concrete surfaces lack visible rainwater management or permeable drainage systems.
aesthetics: Consistent building heights and unified facade designs with traditional-style streetlamps create strong visual coherence.
The street appears highly clean and well-maintained without obvious litter, creating a pleasant visual environment for all users.
The lack of mature street vegetation and the large expanse of monotonous grey asphalt detract slightly from the overall visual appeal.
comfort: The sparse tree canopy provides negligible shade, leading to poor thermal comfort for elderly and disabled pedestrians during hot weather.
The absence of public benches or resting facilities severely reduces physical comfort for older adults who require frequent breaks while walking.
Wide and relatively flat sidewalk surfaces offer a smooth walking path, supporting physical comfort for wheelchair users and pedestrians.
walkability: Generous sidewalk widths allow for unobstructed side-by-side walking and easy passage for wheelchairs and pedestrians.
The lack of marked mid-block crosswalks or pedestrian refuge islands makes crossing the wide street difficult and stressful for older adults and disabled individuals.
Continuous commercial facades keep the walking experience visually engaging and provide immediate destinations, improving walkability.
bikeability: The absence of dedicated or protected bike lanes forces cyclists into shared lanes, significantly lowering perceived and actual safety for adolescent and adult cyclists.
On-street parked cars adjacent to the cycling path pose a continuous 'dooring' hazard and obstruct travel routes for cyclists.
The flat terrain and straight road alignment are physically conducive to cycling, though the lack of safe infrastructure heavily undermines the experience.
